w: Nine centuries of miners hollowing rock salt from the ground, until an underground world took shape: chapels, chandeliers, statues, even a lake, all carved from the mineral itself. Commercial mining ran continuously until 1996 - now a UNESCO site you descend into rather than just visit.
s: An underground salt cathedral, mined for 700 years
_facts: Salt mined from Neolithic times, excavated as a mine from the 13th century
Produced table salt continuously until 1996, one of the world's oldest operating salt mines
UNESCO World Heritage Site and Polish Historic Monument
Attractions include shafts, an underground lake, four chapels, and statues carved by miners from rock salt

w: Nearly a thousand years old and still the coronation church of Polish monarchs, its golden-domed Sigismund's Chapel rated among finest Renaissance work north of the Alps. The day after his 1946 ordination, priest Karol Wojtyla said his first Mass in the crypt below - decades before Pope John Paul II.
_facts: Nearly 1,000 years old, part of the Wawel Castle Complex
National sanctuary and coronation site of Polish monarchs
Contains the golden-domed Sigismund's Chapel
Karol Wojtyla (later Pope John Paul II) said his first Mass in the Wawel Crypt on 2 November 1946

w: A Nazi concentration camp in the Podgorze district, where Polish Jews were held for forced labour amid executions and desperate conditions during the Holocaust - the story later made known worldwide through Schindler's List. It was evacuated in January 1945, only days before the Red Army liberated the area.
s: Nazi camp made infamous by Schindler's List
_facts: German Nazi concentration camp operated by the SS near Plaszow, southern Krakow
Most prisoners were Polish Jews targeted for destruction during the Holocaust
Many died from executions, forced labor, and poor conditions
Camp evacuated January 1945, days before Red Army liberation on 20 January 1945

w: Poland's most historically loaded hill: a fortified royal residence founded on the orders of Casimir the Great, rebuilt across Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque centuries, and still the country's most-visited art museum - over 3.47 million visitors in 2025 alone.
s: Seat of Polish kings on a limestone hill since 970 CE
_facts: Established on the orders of King Casimir III the Great
Most visited art museum in Poland, over 3.47 million visitors in 2025
Oldest stone buildings trace back to 970 CE
First World Heritage Site declared in 1978, part of Historic Centre of Krakow

w: The enamelware works that lent Schindler's List its title and its setting, immortalised on screen as Oskar Schindler's Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik. The administration building in Zablocie now houses a branch of Krakow's Historical Museum, while the old workshops hold the city's Museum of Contemporary Art.
_facts: Former metal item factory in Zablocie, Krakow
Now hosts the Museum of Contemporary Art (former workshops) and a branch of the Historical Museum of Krakow
Featured in the film Schindler's List as Oskar Schindler's Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik (DEF)
Predecessor enamelware company instituted March 1937

w: A museum of historic aircraft on the grounds of one of the world's oldest airfields, laid out by Austria-Hungary in 1912 and flying until 1963. CNN once ranked it among the world's best aviation museums; for half a century its exhibits sat in draughty ex-airfield hangars before a proper hall opened in 2010.
s: Historic planes on one of the world's oldest airfields
_facts: Located at the former Krakow-Rakowice-Czyzyny Airport, established 1912
One of the oldest airfields in the world; airfield closed 1963, museum opened 1964
Listed among the world's best aviation museums by CNN
New main building opened 18 September 2010

w: Krakow's grand 19th-century necropolis, laid out when the city belonged to Austrian Galicia and expanded repeatedly until it now covers some 42 hectares. Wander its avenues of family tombs and you're walking among generations of notable Cracovians, each headstone its own small monument.
_facts: Historic necropolis and cultural heritage monument at 26 Rakowicka Street
Founded early 19th century under Austrian Galicia, expanded several times
Covers about 42 hectares (100 acres)
Many notable Cracovians are buried here

w: Nearly 6.7 million volumes deep, the Jagiellonian University's library holds Copernicus's own manuscript of De Revolutionibus alongside underground samizdat literature smuggled through Poland's communist decades. It also houses the disputed Berlinka collection, whose legal ownership Germany still contests.
s: Copernicus's own manuscript sits on these shelves
_facts: Library of Jagiellonian University in Krakow, almost 6.7 million volumes
Holds Copernicus's autograph manuscript of De Revolutionibus and Dlugosz's Banderia Prutenorum
Large collection of samizdat (drugi obieg) literature from communist-era Poland
Houses the Berlinka art collection, whose legal status is disputed with Germany

w: One of the oldest stone churches in Poland, tucked into a corner of the Main Market Square with almost a thousand years of history reaching back to the dawn of Polish Romanesque architecture. Merchants travelling in from across medieval Europe worshipped here first.
s: Poland's oldest stone church, on the main square
_facts: One of the oldest stone churches in Poland, at the intersection of the Main Market Square and Grodzka Street
Almost 1,000-year history, early Polish Romanesque architecture
Was a place of worship for merchants travelling across medieval Europe
A meeting place for citizens and nobility

w: A golden-domed funerary chapel built for the last Jagiellonian kings, praised by art historians as the finest example of Tuscan Renaissance work north of the Alps. King Sigismund I financed it; Bartolomeo Berrecci built it in 1519-33, and it now holds three royal tombs.
s: The Renaissance masterpiece inside Wawel Cathedral
_facts: Royal chapel of Wawel Cathedral, built as funerary chapel for the last Jagiellonian dynasty members
Hailed as 'the most beautiful example of Tuscan Renaissance north of the Alps'
Financed by King Sigismund I the Old, built 1519-33 by Bartolomeo Berrecci
Houses tombs of King Sigismund I, Sigismund II Augustus, and Anna Jagiellon

w: A museum devoted to Japanese art and technology on the banks of the Vistula in Debniki, built to give a long-growing collection a permanent home. Until 2005 it operated as a branch of the National Museum in Krakow; today it stands alone as an unlikely outpost of Japanese culture in southern Poland.
s: Krakow's museum of Japanese art, on the Vistula
_facts: Museum of Japanese Art and Technology 'Manggha' at 26 M. Konopnickiej Street, Debniki
Until 2005 it was a branch of the National Museum of Krakow

w: A historic Catholic parish and conventual church in Kazimierz, run since its founding by the Canons Regular of the Lateran on Bozego Ciala Street - Corpus Christi Street, its very name folded into the old Jewish quarter's geography.
s: Corpus Christi's church, deep in Kazimierz
_facts: Historic Roman Catholic parish and conventual church of the Canons Regular of the Lateran
Located at 26 Bozego Ciala Street in Kazimierz, former district of Krakow

w: Legend holds this was where Bishop Stanislaus of Krakow was slain on the orders of King Boleslaw the Bold in 1079 - a killing that got the king exiled and the bishop canonised. Known as the Church on the Rock, its crypt now serves as a pantheon for distinguished Poles.
s: Where a king's men killed a bishop-turned-saint
_facts: Historic Roman Catholic conventual church of the Order of Saint Paul the First Hermit, known as Skalka / Church on the Rock
Crypt beneath the church serves as a pantheon to distinguished Poles
Said to be where Saint Stanislaus of Szczepanow was slain by order of King Boleslaw II the Bold in 1079
Led to the king's exile and Stanislaus's eventual canonization

w: A Reform congregation's synagogue in Moorish Revival dress, its horseshoe arches and stencilled interiors completed in 1862 for Krakow's more progressive Jewish community. Concerts still fill it today, especially during the Krakow Jewish Culture Festival, when Kazimierz's old streets come alive.
s: Moorish Revival synagogue for Krakow's Reform Jews
_facts: Reform Jewish congregation and synagogue at 24 Miodowa Street, Kazimierz
Designed by Ignacy Hercok in Moorish Revival and Rundbogenstil styles, completed 1862
Booming centre of Jewish culture, hosts concerts and meetings, especially during the Krakow Jewish Culture Festival

w: A museum of Krakow's deep past, founded in 1850 and quietly filling in the centuries before the written record - the finds that don't get their own guidebook chapter but built the ground the rest of the city stands on.
_facts: Historic museum in Krakow, Lesser Poland Voivodeship
Established in 1850

w: Baroque and built in 1644 for its donor, a wealthy banker to King Wladyslaw IV known simply as Isaac the Rich, whose fortune paid for one of Kazimierz's grandest Orthodox synagogues. Francesco Olivierri's design has weathered nearly four centuries here.
s: Built by a banker known as Isaac the Rich
_facts: Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue at 14 Kupa Street, Kazimierz
Designed by Francesco Olivierri in Baroque style, completed 1644
Named for donor Izaak Jakubowicz, called Isaac the Rich, a banker to King Ladislaus IV of Poland

w: A historic parish and university collegiate church marking the start of Krakow's old Royal Road, at the head of Jan Matejko Square where the medieval market town of Kleparz once stood before being absorbed into the Old Town.
s: Start of Krakow's old Royal Road
_facts: Historic Roman Catholic parish and university collegiate church at 2 Kurniki Street, Kleparz
Stands at the northern end of Jan Matejko Square, former centre of medieval Kleparz
Marks the beginning of the Royal Road

w: Known as the Synagogue of the Poor, built in the 17th century in the district King John I Albert set aside for Krakow's Jewish community in 1495. Nazis devastated it in the war and it saw profane use for decades after; since 1996 it has run as a Jewish museum and festival venue.
s: The Synagogue of the Poor, restored as a museum
_facts: 17th-century former synagogue at 8 Warszauera Street, Kazimierz, also known as Synagogue of the Poor
Neighbourhood earmarked in 1495 by King John I Albert for the Jewish community
Devastated by Nazis in WWII, used for profane purposes until 1991, operated as Jewish museum since 1996
Venue for the annual Jewish Culture Festival in Krakow
